questions.q: A chronicler writes about King Ravi: 'He seized the hill kingdom's iron mines and elephant forests so that his army would never again be outnumbered. In his capital he raised a pillar naming himself ruler of the whole world.' Which pairing of motives for becoming an emperor matches the two parts of the chronicle?
questions.a: The iron mines and elephant forests are about gaining access to resources to build military strength (the chapter's second motive). Calling himself ruler of the whole world is the chapter's metaphor for controlling large territories and being remembered by later generations (the first motive). The other pairings swap the motives or reduce both to wealth.
o: Mines and forests: resources for military strength; the pillar: the wish to be remembered by later generations
Seizing the mines and forests: the wish to be remembered by later generations; the pillar: resources for military strength
Seizing the mines and forests: the desire for great wealth for himself; the pillar: resources for military strength
Both the seizure and the pillar: the desire for great wealth for himself and for the empire

questions.q:
Chitra's notes on a bazaar in a city of a vast territory read: 'A mint stamps one coin used in all the lands. Officers in the market collect tax. An army camp guards the border road. Traders from distant lands sell silk and spices.' She says: 'This proves the state is an empire and not just a kingdom.'
(a) Which feature of an empire does the mint show?
(b) Which features do the tax officers and the army camp show?
(c) Name one feature of the chapter's list that her notes do not mention.
(d) Does her evidence prove an empire? What further evidence would she need, and why?
questions.a: (a) Making laws and issuing currencies, weights and measures. (b) An administration (collecting taxes) and an army. (c) Any one of controlling resources, encouraging art and learning, communication networks, central authority over tributaries. (d) Not yet: a big kingdom may also have a mint and an army. She would need evidence that smaller territories keep their own rulers who pay tribute to the emperor in a capital.
s: Part (a): currency, weights and measures
Part (b): administration and army
Part (c): one unmentioned feature
Part (d): needs tributary rulers paying tribute as evidence

questions.q: 'An empire is held together by more than its army.' Justify the statement using the chapter.
questions.a: The army conquers tributaries and defends borders, but an administration with officials collects taxes and keeps order; laws, currencies and weights regulate trade; roads and river routes carry messages and goods; and encouragement of art, literature, religions and centres of learning is also a feature. The ruler also controls resources such as mines and forests.
s: Role of the army (control, expansion, defence)
Administration: officials, taxes, law and order
Laws, currency, weights and measures, regulating trade
Communication networks and infrastructure
Art, learning and resource control as further supports, with a conclusion

questions.q: Compare the position of an emperor and of a tributary ruler in an empire. Analyse what each gains from the arrangement.
questions.a: The emperor exerts central authority from a capital, receives tribute and loyalty and gains resources and power. The tributary king submits and accepts overlordship, pays tribute, but generally continues to govern his own area. Each gets something: the emperor wealth, power and control, the tributary a measure of self-rule.
s: Emperor: central authority, capital, overlord
Tributary: submits, pays tribute, accepts overlordship
Emperor's gains: tribute, resources, power
Tributary's gain: continues to govern own area
A clear comparison of the two positions

questions.q: A kingdom's hills give timber and elephants, its plains give grain, and its river carries merchant boats. (a) Which two of the resources an emperor controls (mines, forest and agricultural produce, manpower) can you see in this description? (b) Why would an emperor also want to control the river?
questions.a: (a) Forest produce (timber, elephants) and agricultural produce (grain). (b) Controlling rivers and trade networks gives control over precious resources and tax revenue from the trade.
s: Part (a): forest produce and agricultural produce identified
Part (b): control of resources and tax revenue from trade

questions.q: A region has eight territories: the emperor's own homeland; three whose rulers still govern their own lands and send elephants every year; two that were annexed, so that the emperor's own officers now govern them directly; and two that are still independent. By the chapter's meaning of the word, the number of tributaries is ___.
Which pair of observations, taken together, shows that a territory is an empire and not just a large kingdom?
questions.a: An empire is a collection of smaller kingdoms whose own rulers pay tribute to an emperor ruling from a capital. A big army, a mint or a grand palace can belong to any large kingdom, and trading together does not make one ruler the overlord.
o: Several rulers each govern their own lands, yet all send grain and elephants to one capital
One king governs every region through his own officials and keeps a very large standing army
Many small kingdoms trade freely with each other and agree to use the same weights and measures
A king has a mint, a fort with a moat and a palace of several storeys in his own capital city

questions.q:
Assertion (A): Tributary kings in an empire generally continued to govern their own areas.
Reason (R): The emperor ruled the whole territory from a capital, usually a major centre of economic and administrative power.
Choose the correct option.
questions.a: Both are true. The capital fact is about where the emperor ruled from; it does not explain why tributary kings were allowed to keep governing.
o: Both Assertion and Reason are true, but the Reason is not the correct explanation of the Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true, and the Reason is the correct explanation of the Assertion.
The Assertion is true, but the Reason is false.
The Assertion is false, but the Reason is true.

questions.q: The rulers of a hill territory send the emperor this message: 'We will send no more elephants or grain; our king alone rules our hills from now on.' (a) What was the hill territory's position before the message, and what is it trying to become? (b) Which feature of an empire will the emperor probably use to answer, and what does the chapter say that feature is for?
questions.a: (a) It was a tributary (a vassal): its ruler governed his own area and paid tribute to the emperor. It is trying to become independent. (b) The army, which the emperor maintains to keep the tributary states under control (as well as to expand the empire and protect it from outside aggression).
s: Part (a): was a tributary paying tribute; now trying to become independent
Part (b): the army, kept to hold tributary states under control

questions.q: Make up a short example of an empire of your own. Name an emperor, one tributary ruler with the tribute he sends, and the capital. Say which two features of an empire your example shows.
questions.a: Any consistent example, such as Emperor Mitra in capital Suvarnapur, with tributary king Arjun sending grain and elephants; shows tribute with own rulers, and a capital as centre, army or administration.
s: Names emperor, tributary and tribute plausibly
Names a capital as a centre of power
Names two features shown by the example

questions.q: A pupil proposes that an emperor should rule from a remote mountain village because it is safe from attack. (a) Which part of the chapter's description of a capital does the proposal ignore? (b) From Ira's tour of Pataliputra, give one thing that shows the economic side of that description.
questions.a: (a) A capital is usually a major centre of economic and administrative power, not merely a safe place. (b) The bustling main market filled with traders from distant lands, selling silk from China and spices and gems from the south, shows economic power.
s: Part (a): a capital is a major centre of economic and administrative power
Part (b): the main market with traders from distant lands as economic power

questions.q: A state's yearly record has six entries: officers collecting taxes; a mint striking new coins; a garrison posted at the frontier; a standard measure fixed for grain; a school for monks endowed; a river road repaired. Sorting them under the chapter's six features of an empire, the number of different features the record covers is ___.
A pupil says: 'People in an empire all share one language and one way of life, so an emperor never has to encourage art, religion or learning.' Show that this cannot be right, using the chapter.
questions.a: The chapter says empires extended over vast areas with diverse people of differing languages, customs and cultures, so there is no single shared way of life. Encouraging art, literature, religions, schools of thought and centres of learning is one of the six features of an empire, so emperors did do it. The pupil's premise is false and so is the conclusion.
s: Diversity of languages, customs and cultures in an empire
Encouraging art, religions and learning is a listed feature
Conclusion: the pupil's premise and conclusion both fail

questions.q:
Match each situation in Column I with the feature of an empire it shows in Column II.
Column I: 1. Boats and roads are kept in repair so orders and goods move  2. Officers count harvests, collect tax and settle disputes  3. The ruler has a cave carved out for a community of monks  4. A garrison is posted at a fort on the frontier
Column II: a. Maintains an army  b. Designs and maintains an administration  c. Maintains communication networks  d. Encourages religions, schools of thought and learning
questions.a: Roads and boats are communication networks, officers who tax and settle disputes are the administration, carving a cave for monks encourages religion and learning, and a frontier garrison is the army.

questions.q:
Raja Aman rules from his capital Amanpur. The kings of Rudra and Soma still govern their own lands but send him grain and elephants every year. Tej was conquered, its king was removed, and Aman's own officers now govern it.
Statement 1: Tej is a tributary of Aman because it also lost a war to him.
Statement 2: Rudra and Soma are tributaries of Aman, a status the chapter also calls being a vassal.
Statement 3: The grain and elephants from Rudra and Soma are tribute, a sign of submission, loyalty or respect to Aman.
Which statements are correct?
questions.a: Statements 2 and 3 are correct. Statement 1 is false: a tributary is a ruler or state that keeps its own ruler and pays tribute; Tej has no ruler of its own now and is governed directly, so losing a war is not what makes a tributary.
o: 2 and 3 only
1 and 2 only
1 and 3 only
1, 2 and 3

questions.q: Ira says her king's authority 'extends over many villages, towns and kingdoms' and that it takes close to two months on horseback to reach the borders. (a) Which one of 'villages, towns, kingdoms' separates an empire from a very large kingdom, and why? (b) What must be true of the rulers of those kingdoms for the chapter's meaning of empire to hold?
questions.a: (a) Kingdoms: an empire is a collection of smaller kingdoms or territories under a powerful ruler, whereas villages and towns also exist inside any large kingdom. (b) They still have their own rulers, who are tributaries to the emperor and pay him tribute.
s: Part (a): kingdoms, since an empire is a collection of smaller kingdoms
Part (b): their rulers remain but are tributaries paying tribute

questions.q: True or False: Since an empire's army exists to defend its borders from enemies, an emperor does not need it to deal with his own tributary kings. Give a reason or the correct statement.
questions.a: False. The chapter says the army is also maintained to keep the tributary states under control and to expand the empire, as well as to protect it from outside aggression.
s: Verdict: False
Correct statement: the army keeps tributaries under control and expands the empire as well as defending it

questions.q: An emperor decrees that only royal agents may cut timber in the hill forests or work the iron mines, that a fixed number of men from each district must serve in his work gangs, and that a share of every district's harvest be reserved for him. Which single feature of an empire do these orders mainly show?
questions.a: Timber and mines (forests and minerals), men for work gangs (manpower) and a share of the harvest (agricultural produce) are the very resources the chapter says an emperor controls and regulates access to. Officials, laws and the army are other features.
o: Controlling and regulating access to mines, forests, agricultural produce and manpower
Designing and maintaining an administration with officials to collect taxes and keep law and order
Making laws, issuing currencies and fixing weights and measures to regulate trade
Maintaining an army to keep the tributary states under control or to expand the empire

questions.q:
Raja Suryadev of Suryapur is thinking of turning his kingdom into an empire. One minister says: 'Your name will be remembered for generations.' Another says: 'The hills around us hold mines and forests that can make us strong.' A third says: 'The neighbouring kingdoms' wealth will fill our treasury.' The treasurer warns that governing many distant territories needs a large army and many officials.
(a) Which two of the chapter's motives for becoming an emperor do the first and second ministers voice?
(b) Which two things must an empire keep up, as the treasurer warns?
(c) Should Suryadev expand? Give one reason for and one cost against, using the chapter.
questions.a: (a) The first minister voices the ambition to rule the world and be remembered by posterity; the second voices access to resources for economic and military strength. (b) An army and an administration (officials to manage territories, collect taxes, maintain law and order). (c) A reasoned decision citing one chapter motive (resources, wealth, ambition) and one cost (army, administration, difficulty of holding a large empire together).
s: Part (a): posterity and access to resources matched to the first and second ministers
Part (b): army and administration
Part (c): a decision citing one motive and one cost from the chapter

questions.q: Rahul says: 'The emperor ruled the whole territory from his capital and kept officials to manage it, so in an empire every area was run by the emperor's own officers and no area kept a ruler of its own.' Is Rahul right? Give reasons.
questions.a: Partly right. He is right that the emperor ruled the whole from a capital and maintained an administration with officials to manage the territories and collect taxes. He is wrong that no area kept its own ruler: the smaller territories still had their own rulers, who were tributaries, and emperors generally allowed regional kings to continue to govern their areas in return for tribute and loyalty.
s: Verdict: partly right
What is right: capital and administration with officials
What is wrong: tributary territories kept their own rulers

questions.q: Four small kingdoms fight for control of a river valley. Kingdom A has the largest army but its fields yield less grain than its people eat. Kingdom B has a large grain surplus but only a small army. Kingdom C has both a strong army and a surplus of grain and timber. Kingdom D has neither. Going by the chapter's account of how an empire arises from warring kingdoms, which is most likely to become the overlord?
questions.a: The chapter's figure notes say that with many smaller kingdoms warring for control, the one with access to stronger military power and surplus resources would eventually become the overlord. Only C has both.
o: Kingdom C, which combines military strength with surplus resources
Kingdom A, because military strength alone decides who becomes overlord
Kingdom B, because surplus resources alone decide who becomes overlord
Kingdom D, because a weak kingdom is rarely attacked and so lasts the longest

questions.q: A town's cloth guild settles its own disputes fairly and the town's trade is flourishing. A royal adviser urges the king to throw out the guild's rules and make royal ones. Which advice fits the chapter's picture of an enlightened ruler?
questions.a: The chapter says guilds had the autonomy to create their own rules and the king was not to interfere, and that an enlightened ruler lets people organise themselves when local institutions work satisfactorily. The other advice breaks that autonomy or the collaboration that made guilds useful.
o: Leave the guild to run its own affairs while its institutions work well
Replace the guild's elected head with an officer chosen by the king himself
Ban guilds and let each trader bargain alone to push the prices all down
Take over the guild's rules so that the army can be fed from its stores

questions.q: The traders of a market town have an association whose members make their own rules for stall sizes and settle quarrels, and the town council keeps out of it because the market is thriving. (a) Which ancient institution of the chapter does it resemble? (b) The chapter names two things that made that institution remarkable. Which of the two does the council's keeping out illustrate, and what reason does the chapter give for the king's not interfering?
questions.a: (a) A guild (shreni). (b) Its autonomy: guilds could create their own internal rules and the king was not to interfere. The chapter's reason is that there is no need to interfere if trade flourishes (an enlightened ruler lets people organise themselves while local institutions work satisfactorily).
s: Part (a): guild (shreni)
Part (b): autonomy to make its own rules, king not to interfere because trade flourished

questions.q: A king plans a long campaign far from home. Soldiers must be fed, clothed, equipped and paid, and elephants and horses cared for, but his treasury is low. Which step does the chapter's reasoning support for raising money in the long run?
questions.a: The chapter says production and trade bring more income for producers and increased tax for the ruler, and that guilds helped trade flourish. Raising tribute is a different, short-term method, and the chapter does not present it as the way to pay for armies.
o: Encourage production and trade so that more tax comes in
Close the trade routes so that all goods stay inside his kingdom
Abolish guilds so that merchants compete against each other
Raise the tribute demanded from the conquered kings

questions.q:
A king plans a 90-day campaign. His clerk's bill lists: food, cloth and pay for 5,000 soldiers at 3 coins a day each, and fodder for 200 elephants at 20 coins a day each. Caravan tax on the trade routes brings in about 8,000 coins a day.
(a) Which army costs named in the chapter are missing from the clerk's bill?
(b) What is the total bill for 90 days, and how much of it does the caravan tax cover?
(c) The minister suggests postponing the campaign to improve trade, or asking tributaries for more tribute. Which would you advise, and why?
questions.a: (a) Weapons and equipment, care of horses, and building roads or ships. (b) Soldiers 5000 x 3 x 90 = 13,50,000; elephants 200 x 20 x 90 = 3,60,000; total 17,10,000 coins; tax 8000 x 90 = 7,20,000, leaving 9,90,000 uncovered. (c) Either, with reasons: postponing lets production and trade grow, which raises income and tax; more tribute is quicker but can burden local rulers and breed resentment.
s: Part (a): equipment, horses or roads and ships missing from the bill
Part (b): 17,10,000 total and 7,20,000 covered
Part (c): a justified decision using trade income or tribute resentment

questions.q: True or False: A king closes his roads to outside merchants to protect his own producers. By the chapter's reasoning he is likely to lose tax income that could have helped pay for his army. Give a reason or the correct statement.
questions.a: True. The chapter links more trade, in greater quantity and variety of goods, to more income for producers and increased tax collections for the ruler, and says an army is costly and needs considerable economic power. Closing the roads cuts the goods traded and so the tax.
s: Verdict: True
Reason: less trade means less tax, while an army needs economic power

questions.q: Write a short notice that a guild in a trading town might put up, showing how it was organised. Mention who leads it, who helps him and one rule the guild makes for itself.
questions.a: A notice such as: 'The guild of Kaveri port is led by its elected head Kumaran with two executive officers; no member may sell below the agreed price of pepper.' It shows an elected head, executive officers and a self-made rule.
s: Names an elected head
Names executive officers
Gives an internal rule the guild itself makes

questions.q: Evaluate the claim: 'Guilds helped both the traders and the king.' Give two points for each.
questions.a: Traders: they collaborated rather than competed, shared information, and made their own rules with an elected head. The king: flourishing trade brought more tax, and he did not have to interfere, which an enlightened ruler would avoid when institutions work. Guilds endured for centuries, so both gained.
s: Trader point 1: collaboration and sharing information
Trader point 2: autonomy and elected head
King point 1: more trade means more tax
King point 2: no need to interfere in working institutions
Judgement that both gained, with evidence of long life

questions.q: 'Production and trade are as important as the army for running an empire.' Justify this statement.
questions.a: An army is costly: soldiers must be fed, clothed, equipped and paid, elephants and horses cared for, roads or ships built. This needs economic power. Controlling trade routes increases the goods traded, income of producers and the ruler's tax. Goods like textiles, spices and gems moved by land and sea, and guilds organised the traders, so a flourishing economy paid for the army.
s: Army is costly: names expenses
Economic power is needed to meet them
Trade routes and goods raise income and taxes
Guilds organised traders and helped trade flourish
Concludes that the army depends on the economy

questions.q: A king lets a flourishing guild go on making its own rules instead of imposing royal ones, because the local institution works satisfactorily. The chapter's adjective for such a ruler is '___ ruler'.
questions.a: enlightened

questions.q: King A taxes 1 coin in every 5 on goods moving on his roads, but traders avoid his roads and goods worth only 10,000 coins pass in a month. King B taxes 1 coin in every 10, but busy guilds and trade routes bring goods worth 40,000 coins a month. (a) Which king collects more tax in a month, and how much does each collect? (b) Which idea of the chapter explains why the lighter tax still brings in more?
questions.a: (a) King B: 40,000 / 10 = 4,000 coins, against King A's 10,000 / 5 = 2,000 coins. (b) More trade means more income for producers and increased tax collections for the ruler, so the amount of trade matters as much as the rate.
s: Part (a): King B with 4,000 against King A's 2,000
Part (b): more trade means increased tax collections for the ruler

questions.q: A king's clerk lists four groups in a town. Which one could NOT be called a guild in the chapter's sense?
questions.a: A guild was an association of traders, craftsmen, moneylenders or agriculturists, usually led by an elected head, that made its own internal rules and shared information. Soldiers under a king-appointed commander have neither a head they chose nor rules of their own.
o: Royal soldiers whose commander the king appoints and who follow his orders
Moneylenders who choose a head and appoint officers to run their trade
Weavers who agree among themselves the rules for selling their cloth
Farmers who pool news of markets and the number of workers available at harvest

questions.q:
Assertion (A): Members of a trade guild shared information on markets, supply and demand and workforce.
Reason (R): Many Indian goods travelled towards distant countries by land or sea.
Choose the correct option.
questions.a: Both are true. The chapter does say Indian goods travelled to distant countries, but that fact does not explain why guild members shared information with each other; the reason given is that sharing was to everyone's benefit.
o: Both Assertion and Reason are true, but the Reason is not the correct explanation of the Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true, and the Reason is the correct explanation of the Assertion.
The Assertion is true, but the Reason is false.
The Assertion is false, but the Reason is true.

questions.q: A village's potters begin selling pots along a new river route to towns downstream, and their incomes rise. (a) Besides the potters, who else gains directly from this trade, according to the chapter, and how? (b) Why does the chapter say a good ruler should care about such production and trade beyond the tax it brings?
questions.a: (a) The ruler: more trade means more income for the producers and increased tax collections for the ruler. (b) Economic activity, especially production and trade, is a key to maintaining an empire and it ensures people's welfare and quality of life, which a good ruler should be concerned with.
s: Part (a): the ruler gains increased tax collections
Part (b): production and trade ensure people's welfare and quality of life

questions.q:
Read the statements about guilds.
Statement 1: Guilds brought together people who ended up as collaborators rather than competitors.
Statement 2: Guilds were associations only of traders, and not of craftsmen, moneylenders or agriculturists.
Statement 3: Guilds spread over large parts of India and endured for centuries.
Which statements are correct?
questions.a: Statements 1 and 3 are correct. Statement 2 is false: the chapter says guilds were powerful associations of traders, craftsmen, moneylenders or agriculturists.
o: 1 and 3 only
1 and 2 only
2 and 3 only
1, 2 and 3

questions.q:
Match each situation in Column I with the chapter idea it shows in Column II.
Column I: 1. A king keeps out of a trade body's rules because trade is flourishing  2. Potters and merchants share news of which markets want their goods  3. Roads to a port are improved and tax from the goods grows  4. Village committees keep on settling local matters themselves
Column II: a. Self-organising ability of Indian society  b. Collaborators rather than competitors  c. Trade routes raise the ruler's income  d. Autonomy of guilds
questions.a: Non-interference shows guild autonomy, sharing market news shows collaborators rather than competitors, better routes raise tax for the ruler, and village committees show the self-organising ability of Indian society.

questions.q: A toll post records the goods passing in one month, in coins: cotton cloth 30,000; pepper 20,000; barley 12,000; cut gems 10,000; horses 8,000. The ruler takes 1 coin in every 10. (a) Group the goods under the chapter's categories (textiles, spices, agricultural produce, luxury items, animals) and say which category yields the most tax and how much. (b) A new road doubles only the barley traded. Which category now yields the second-largest tax?
questions.a: (a) Cloth is textiles (30,000), pepper is a spice (20,000), barley is agricultural produce (12,000), gems are luxury items (10,000), horses are animals (8,000). Textiles give the most: 30,000 / 10 = 3,000 coins. (b) Barley becomes 24,000, which beats spices at 20,000, so agricultural produce is second, yielding 2,400 coins.
s: Part (a): textiles highest with 3,000 coins
Part (b): agricultural produce second with 24,000 traded

questions.q: A minister says: 'Spending on trade routes is a waste, because only the traders gain from trade.' Is he right? Give reasons from the chapter.
questions.a: No. The chapter says more trade means more income for the producers, but it also means increased tax collections for the ruler, and economic activity ensures people's welfare and quality of life, which a good ruler should be concerned with. So the benefit is shared by producers, ruler and people.
s: Verdict: not right
Gain to ruler: increased tax collections
Gain to people: welfare and quality of life

questions.q: Anita says: 'Guilds made traders who might have been competitors into collaborators, and that is why guilds lasted for centuries.' Is she completely right? Give reasons.
questions.a: Partly. The chapter says guilds brought together people who ended up as collaborators rather than competitors, and that they spread widely and endured for centuries. But it names a second remarkable feature, autonomy to make their own rules, and does not say that collaboration alone was the reason for their long life.
s: Verdict: right about collaboration, not completely right
Supports: collaborators rather than competitors; guilds endured for centuries
Limit: autonomy is the second feature, and the chapter does not give one reason for their long life

questions.q:
Two river-port towns each have 60 cloth-makers. In Town A they sell separately and keep markets and workforce news to themselves; 2,000 bolts of cloth are sold in a season. In Town B the cloth-makers and local moneylenders chose a head and meet to share what they know about markets, supply and demand and workers; 3,200 bolts are sold in the same season. A bolt sells for 40 coins and the king takes 1 coin in every 10.
(a) What does the chapter call the body formed in Town B, and how was its head usually chosen?
(b) What did sharing information turn the members from, and into?
(c) How much more tax does the king get from Town B than from Town A, and which idea of the chapter links that to trade?
(d) A royal officer wants to take over Town B's rules and appoint its head 'to collect tax more efficiently'. Advise the king, using the chapter.
questions.a: (a) A guild (shreni); its head was usually elected. (b) From competitors into collaborators. (c) Town A: 2,000 x 40 / 10 = 8,000 coins; Town B: 3,200 x 40 / 10 = 12,800 coins; 4,800 coins more. More trade means increased tax collections for the ruler. (d) Do not take over: guilds had the autonomy to make their own rules and the king was not to interfere, and an enlightened ruler refrains from interfering while a local institution works satisfactorily; Town B's larger trade and tax show that it is working.
s: Part (a): guild and elected head
Part (b): competitors into collaborators
Part (c): 4,800 coins more, because more trade means more tax
Part (d): leave it alone, citing autonomy, non-interference and flourishing trade

questions.q:
Assertion (A): Traders joined together in guilds instead of working only as isolated individuals.
Reason (R): Sharing resources and information on markets, supply and demand and workforce was to everyone's benefit.
Choose the correct option.
questions.a: Both are true and R explains A: the benefits of sharing information and resources are why traders joined forces.
o: Both Assertion and Reason are true, and the Reason is the correct explanation of the Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true, but the Reason is not the correct explanation of the Assertion.
The Assertion is true, but the Reason is false.
The Assertion is false, but the Reason is true.

questions.q:
In a village of 50 families in Magadha, each family harvested 40 sacks of grain a year and needed 38 for itself. After 20 families took up iron-tipped ploughs, those 20 families harvested 55 sacks each, while the other 30 families still harvested 40. Assume the local chief collects the extra grain produced by the new ploughs.
(a) What does the chapter say iron ploughs did for agriculture?
(b) Find the village's total surplus before and after the 20 families changed their ploughs.
(c) What does the chapter say a food surplus allows people to do?
(d) The chief can use the extra grain either to support more soldiers with iron weapons or about 7 craftsman families (taking 38 sacks to feed a family). Which would you recommend, and why?
questions.a: (a) They increased agricultural produce. (b) Before: 50 x 2 = 100 sacks. After: 20 x 17 + 30 x 2 = 340 + 60 = 400 sacks. (c) More people can focus on arts and crafts, which are in demand inside and outside the empire. (d) 300 sacks feed 7 whole families at 38 sacks each. Either, with reasons: craftsmen produce goods for trade and raise income, which the chapter links to Magadha's rise; soldiers with iron weapons strengthen the army.
s: Part (a): iron ploughs raised produce
Part (b): 100 sacks before and 400 after
Part (c): surplus lets people focus on arts and crafts
Part (d): a justified choice using the chapter

questions.q:
Read the statements about Magadha and the Nandas.
Statement 1: Ajatashatru helped make Magadha a dominant centre of power, and the Buddha and Mahavira lived in his time.
Statement 2: Mahapadma Nanda united many smaller kingdoms and extended his empire across parts of eastern and northern India.
Statement 3: Mahapadma Nanda founded the Nanda dynasty around the 4th century BCE.
Which statements are correct?
questions.a: The first two statements are correct. The third is false: the chapter places Mahapadma Nanda around the 5th century BCE.
o: 1 and 2 only
2 and 3 only
1 and 3 only
1, 2 and 3

questions.q: Panini, who lived around the 5th century BCE in the time of the Nandas, set out the rules of Sanskrit grammar in 3,996 short sutras. A teacher wants her class to pass these rules on from generation to generation. (a) Why do short sutras suit that aim? (b) The Nanda age also left punch-marked coins. Say what the grammar and the coins each tell a historian about that age.
questions.a: (a) Sutras are concise, carefully crafted phrases that capture knowledge and important ideas in a way that is easy to remember and pass on. (b) The coins show economic power: Mahapadma Nanda began issuing coins as the economy thrived. The grammar shows that a major work on Sanskrit grammar was composed in the Nanda age, an achievement of learning beside the economic one.
s: Part (a): sutras are concise and easy to remember and pass on
Part (b): coins show economic power; the grammar shows a work of learning in that age

questions.q: A king of Magadha can first spend his limited iron on plough tips for villagers or on weapons for soldiers. (a) What would each choice do first, according to the chapter? (b) Why did Magadha's rise need both?
questions.a: (a) Plough tips would raise agricultural produce; weapons would strengthen the army. (b) A larger farm surplus allowed more people to take up crafts and trade, which brought income, and a strong army was needed to expand and unify kingdoms; the chapter ties both to the use of iron.
s: Part (a): iron ploughs raise produce, iron weapons strengthen the army
Part (b): surplus and trade income and army strength both fed Magadha's rise

questions.q: A dynasty founded in the 5th century BCE (take it as 500 to 401 BCE) ended around 321 BCE when the Mauryas took over. It can have ruled for at most ___ years.
Describe a short imagined scene from a Magadhan village that shows how iron ploughs could end up raising the king's income. Show at least three links in the chain.
questions.a: A scene such as: an iron plough digs deeper, harvest rises, extra grain lets a family's son become a potter, pots are carried down the Son river and sold, and the king collects more income. It shows ploughs, surplus, crafts and trade as links.
s: Iron plough raises produce
Surplus lets people work in crafts
Trade by river raises income

questions.q: Rahul says: 'The Nanda empire fell because it was poor and had no army.' Do you agree? Give reasons from the chapter.
questions.a: No. Dhana Nanda was very rich, and Greek accounts say the Nandas kept a large army. The chapter says he became highly unpopular because he oppressed and exploited his people, which paved the way for the Mauryas to conquer and absorb the empire.
s: Verdict: disagrees
Evidence: the last ruler was rich and the Nandas had a large army
Cause given by the chapter: unpopularity from oppression and exploitation

questions.q: A museum shuffles four cards about Magadha's rulers. Card P: 'Founded a dynasty and began issuing coins as the economy thrived.' Card Q: 'Lived when the Buddha and Mahavira lived and made Magadha a dominant centre of power.' Card R: 'The founder of the Maurya empire.' Card S: 'Very rich but highly unpopular; his empire was absorbed by the Mauryas.' Which order puts them from earliest to latest, using the chapter?
questions.a: Ajatashatru (Card Q) belongs to the early kings of Magadha; Mahapadma Nanda (Card P) founded the Nanda dynasty; Dhana Nanda (Card S) was its last emperor, whose empire was then absorbed by the Maurya empire founded by Chandragupta (Card R).
o: Q, P, S, R
P, Q, S, R
Q, P, R, S
Q, S, P, R

questions.q: Suppose a drought ruins the grain harvest of the Ganga plains for three years running. Using only the chain of reasons the chapter gives for Magadha's rise, predict three consequences in the order they would follow.
questions.a: First, agricultural produce falls, so the surplus food grains shrink. Second, fewer people can give up farming to focus on arts and crafts, so goods for trade fall. Third, with less trade the income of the kingdom drops, which weakens the base on which Magadha's rise rested.
s: Produce and the surplus of food grains fall
Fewer people can focus on arts and crafts, so fewer goods for trade
Less trade means less income for the kingdom

questions.q: Suppose the hills near Magadha had held no iron ore, though its plains, forests and rivers were as before. Which loss would the chapter's reasoning predict most directly?
questions.a: The chapter says iron ore and other minerals from the nearby hilly regions were crucial: iron ploughs increased agricultural produce and lighter, sharper iron weapons strengthened the army. The rivers, forests and fertile land are separate advantages that would remain.
o: Iron ploughs for produce and iron weapons for the army
The Ganga and Son rivers as a means of carrying goods for trade
The timber and the elephants that the forests supplied to armies
The fertile land of the Ganga plains on which villages farmed

questions.q: (a) Sort these into natural advantages and human actions behind Magadha's rise: iron ore in nearby hills; the iron plough; Ajatashatru's leadership; the Ganga and Son rivers. (b) Explain how one human action depended on one natural advantage.
questions.a: (a) Natural advantages: iron ore in the hills and the Ganga and Son rivers. Human actions: the iron plough and Ajatashatru's leadership. (b) Iron ploughs and weapons were made possible by iron ore from nearby hills (or trade by river depended on the rivers being used for transport).
s: Part (a): natural advantages and human actions sorted correctly
Part (b): a human action linked to the natural advantage it depended on

questions.q: Magadha's rise is explained in the chapter by the fertile Ganga plains, forests with timber and elephants, iron ore from nearby hills, rivers for transport, and strong early kings. Choose the ONE factor you think mattered most for Magadha becoming the base of India's first empire. Support your choice with the chapter's evidence, and say why the strongest rival factor mattered less.
questions.a: A reasoned choice, for example iron: iron ploughs increased agricultural produce, the surplus let more people focus on arts and crafts, and lighter, sharper iron weapons strengthened the army, so one resource worked on both farming and war. The strongest rival, the rivers, boosted trade and income, but the goods that trade carried came from the produce and crafts that the iron-based surplus made possible. (Choosing the rivers and treating iron as the rival is equally acceptable if argued from the chapter.)
s: Names one factor clearly
Chapter evidence for it, first point
Chapter evidence for it, second point
Names the strongest rival factor and what it did
Explains why the rival mattered less

questions.q: Two students read about the Nandas. Gita says the coins prove Mahapadma Nanda was powerful. Hari says the Greek accounts of his large army prove it. (a) What does each kind of evidence show on its own? (b) Why is the claim stronger when both are used together with the extent of his empire?
questions.a: (a) Coins show economic power; the Greek accounts show military strength. (b) Together with his unification of many smaller kingdoms across parts of eastern and northern India they show economic, military and political strength, so the claim does not rest on one piece of evidence.
s: Part (a): coins as economic power, army accounts as military power
Part (b): several kinds of evidence together support the claim

questions.q:
Match each piece of evidence in Column I with what the chapter says it shows in Column II.
Column I: 1. A punch-marked silver coin of Mahapadma Nanda  2. Greek accounts of the Nandas  3. The 3,996 sutras of Panini's Ashtadhyayi  4. Iron ploughs and iron weapons in Magadha
Column II: a. The Nandas maintained a large army  b. The economy thrived and the ruler could show economic power  c. Knowledge set in short phrases that are easy to remember and pass on  d. Higher agricultural produce and a stronger army
questions.a: A coin that the ruler could issue shows a thriving economy and economic power; Greek accounts tell of the large Nanda army; sutras are concise phrases easy to remember and pass on; iron ploughs raised produce and iron weapons strengthened the army.

questions.q: A trader of Rajagriha sends cloth to a market town by boat on the Ganga. Which advantage of his kingdom's geography is he using, and how does it help the king?
questions.a: The chapter says the Ganga and Son gave a geographical advantage for trade because they could be used for transportation, and the flourishing trade boosted income. Iron ore came from hilly regions; elephants and timber came from forests.
o: The rivers as a way to carry goods, which raises trade and income
The rivers as a source of the iron ore used for weapons and ploughs
The rivers as a source of the elephants used in the army's campaigns
The rivers as a source of the timber cut in the nearby forests

questions.q: A panel at Sanchi shows soldiers on elephants, soldiers on horses and soldiers on foot besieging the city of Kusinara, while the Buddha's relics are carried away on an elephant. Which statement is supported by the chapter's text about Magadha but cannot be read off the panel as described?
questions.a: The panel as described shows elephant riders, horse riders and foot soldiers, and the relics on an elephant. It says nothing about the metal of the weapons; that iron weapons made armies stronger and that iron ore came from nearby hilly regions is stated in the chapter's text.
o: Lighter, sharper iron weapons strengthened armies; the ore came from nearby hills
Soldiers on elephants took part in the siege of the city, beside the horse riders
Foot soldiers and horse riders attacked the same city together in one siege
The casket holding the Buddha's relics was carried off from the city on an elephant

questions.q:
A museum plans a Nanda gallery. Asha says: 'The Nandas had coins, a large army and a great grammarian in their age.' Bilal says: 'Their last emperor was unpopular, and another dynasty took over his lands.'
(a) Which facts in the chapter support Asha: name the coin issuer, the source of the army fact and the grammarian?
(b) Which facts support Bilal, and which dynasty took over?
(c) The gallery must choose a heading: 'A Rich and Powerful Empire' or 'An Unpopular Empire that Fell'. Which would you choose, and why?
questions.a: (a) Mahapadma Nanda issued coins; Greek accounts mention the large army; Panini composed the Ashtadhyayi. (b) Dhana Nanda, though very rich, oppressed and exploited his people and was highly unpopular; the Maurya Empire absorbed the Nanda empire. (c) Either, with reasons: the first heading fits coins, army and wealth; the second fits the oppression, unpopularity and the Mauryan conquest.
s: Part (a): coins, Greek accounts, Panini
Part (b): Dhana Nanda's unpopularity and the Mauryas
Part (c): a justified heading using both sets of facts

questions.q: True or False: The Ganga and Son rivers helped Magadha rise mainly by supplying the iron ore for its ploughs and weapons. Give the correct statement if false.
questions.a: False. The iron ore came from nearby hilly regions; the Ganga and Son gave a geographical advantage for trade because they could be used for transportation, which boosted the empire's income.
s: Verdict: False
Correct statement: iron ore came from the hills and the rivers carried goods for trade

questions.q: Forty Magadhan families each used to harvest 40 sacks of grain a year. After they take up iron-tipped ploughs each harvests 50 sacks. A family of craftsmen, who grow no grain, needs 38 sacks a year. If the whole extra harvest is used to feed craftsman families, how many whole families can the village now support?
questions.a: The extra harvest is 40 x (50 - 40) = 400 sacks, and 400 / 38 is about 10.5, so 10 whole families. Surplus food grains are what allowed more people to focus on arts and crafts. Eleven families would need 418 sacks; 40 would be one craftsman family for every farming family.
o: 10 families
11 families
4 families
40 families

questions.q: 'The Nanda empire fell because of its ruler's conduct, not because it lacked wealth or arms.' Evaluate this statement with evidence from the chapter.
questions.a: Mahapadma Nanda united kingdoms, issued coins and kept a large army, and the last emperor, Dhana Nanda, was very rich. These show wealth and arms. But Dhana Nanda became highly unpopular because he oppressed and exploited the people, which paved the way for the Mauryas to conquer and absorb the empire. So the statement is mostly supported, though other causes may also have played a part.
s: Evidence of Nanda wealth: coins, rich Dhana Nanda
Evidence of arms: large army per Greek accounts
Dhana Nanda's oppression and unpopularity
Link to the Maurya conquest
A balanced judgement on the statement

questions.q:
Assertion (A): The Ganga and Son rivers were the main reason for the strength of Magadha's army, since they supplied the iron ore for its weapons.
Reason (R): The Ganga and Son rivers could be used for transportation, which gave Magadha a geographical advantage for trade.
Choose the correct option.
questions.a: The Assertion is false: the chapter says iron ore and other minerals came from the nearby hilly regions, not from the rivers. The Reason is true as the chapter states it, but it concerns trade, not weapons.
o: The Assertion is false, but the Reason is true.
Both Assertion and Reason are true, and the Reason is the correct explanation of the Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true, but the Reason is not the correct explanation of the Assertion.
The Assertion is true, but the Reason is false.

questions.q: Dev says: 'The Persian Empire links Alexander's war in the west to his coming to India: he attacked Persia to avenge its earlier invasions of Greece, and some Indian soldiers from the Persian-ruled north-west had fought against Greeks in those invasions.' Is Dev right? Give reasons.
questions.a: Yes. The chapter says Alexander campaigned against the Persian Empire to avenge earlier Persian invasions of Greece, and that in those invasions some Indian soldiers from the Persian-ruled north-west fought against Greeks. The limit is that the chapter gives a different spur for his push into India (he was eager to reach 'the end of the world'), so the link is the Persian Empire, not revenge.
s: Verdict: right
Both facts: revenge for Persian invasions, and Indian soldiers from the Persian-ruled north-west fighting Greeks
Limit: his push into India is given a different motive

questions.q: Greek records say that in a few battles in India 'women fought side by side with their men', and that Alexander massacred the population of several cities. (a) What do these two reports together suggest about how Alexander's army was received? (b) Name two later events in the chapter that this response helps to explain.
questions.a: (a) Local tribes and rulers put up fierce resistance; many people fought hard and did not welcome him. (b) Alexander himself was seriously wounded in a battle, and his tired, homesick soldiers lost the will to fight and refused to move deeper into India, so the campaign turned back.
s: Part (a): fierce resistance from local people
Part (b): two of: Alexander wounded, soldiers lost the will to fight, refusal to go on

questions.q: A student writes: 'The Gymnosophists were Indian sages who called themselves naked philosophers.' Which correction fits the chapter?
questions.a: The chapter says the Greeks called the sages 'Gymnosophists' or 'naked philosophers', probably because they wore very little clothing, and that they were renowned for their wisdom. It was the Greeks' label, not the sages' own name; the other options invent a punishment, a council and a reversal.
o: The Greeks named them so, probably because they wore very little; they were renowned for wisdom
Alexander gave them that name as a punishment once they failed to answer his riddles correctly
It was the Sanskrit title of the ruling council of the Pauravas, the people led by Porus himself
Indians used it for the Greek philosophers who travelled with Alexander's army to the Indus

questions.q:
Assertion (A): Alexander's campaign in north-west India is said to have had limited political impact.
Reason (R): It opened the door for Indo-Greek cultural contacts.
Choose the correct option.
questions.a: Both are true, but contact in culture is a different effect and does not explain why the political impact was limited.
o: Both Assertion and Reason are true, but the Reason is not the correct explanation of the Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true, and the Reason is the correct explanation of the Assertion.
The Assertion is true, but the Reason is false.
The Assertion is false, but the Reason is true.

questions.q: A student's timeline says: 'In 322 BCE Alexander was fighting Porus in Punjab.' Show that this cannot be right.
questions.a: The chapter dates his India campaign to 327-325 BCE, his time back in Persia to 324-323 BCE, and says he died in Babylon at the age of 32. 322 BCE is after that, so he could not have been fighting in Punjab.
s: States the campaign dates 327-325 BCE
States the Persian period ending 323 BCE and his death in Babylon
Concludes 322 BCE is impossible

questions.q: True or False: The story of Alexander sparing the Gymnosophists after they answered his riddles calmly is read by historians as a meeting of Greek and Indian philosophies, so it can serve as evidence of cultural contact even though his political impact in India was limited. Give a reason or the correct statement.
questions.a: True. The chapter says Alexander was impressed and spared them all, that historians view such exchanges as a meeting of two great traditions, Greek and Indian philosophies, and that his campaign in north-west India had limited political impact but opened the door for Indo-Greek cultural contacts.
s: Verdict: True
Reason: historians read the exchange as a meeting of two traditions, while political impact was limited

questions.q: (a) Give one fact from the chapter that explains why historians of the world rank Alexander highly. (b) Using the chapter's reasoning about large empires, explain why an empire like his was unlikely to outlast him.
questions.a: (a) He conquered the Persian Empire and his empire spread over three continents, one of the largest in world history (or: the influence of Greek culture spread). (b) The larger an empire, the more difficult it is to hold together, and far-off territories are often the first to split away; after he died his empire was soon divided between his generals and the satraps.
s: Part (a): one valid fact such as conquest of Persia or three continents
Part (b): large empires are hard to hold together and far areas split first

questions.q: Alexander warned the Gymnosophists that he would put to death those who gave wrong answers, yet he spared them all. Analyse what this episode, with the two exchanges the chapter quotes, shows about the encounter of Greek and Indian traditions, and why a historian should be careful in using the story as evidence.
questions.a: The sages answered calmly and intelligently, and the replies gave reasons: life is stronger than death because it endures, and a man is most loved if he is powerful yet does not inspire fear, perhaps a hint to the mighty ruler. Alexander was impressed and spared them, so the meeting ended in respect rather than force; historians view such exchanges as a meeting of Greek and Indian philosophies. But the story is told 'according to one account' and different versions have been told over the centuries, so it shows the kind of contact, not exact words or events.
s: Threat answered by calm, intelligent replies
An example of a reply with its reason
Alexander impressed and spared them
Historians' view: a meeting of two great traditions
Caution: different versions, one account

questions.q: (a) How does a satrap differ from a tributary ruler in the way the chapter describes them? (b) Which of the two was Porus after the battle in Punjab, and why?
questions.a: (a) A satrap is a governor or official left behind by the overlord to manage far-off territory, while a tributary is a ruler or state that has submitted to an emperor and pays him tribute. (b) A satrap, because Alexander left him at the head of his kingdom in that role.
s: Part (a): satrap as a governor left by an overlord, tributary as a ruler paying tribute
Part (b): Porus as satrap, with the reason from the chapter

questions.q: Alexander's campaign in India ended in 325 BCE. Using the chapter's date for the emergence of the Maurya Empire, the Mauryas appeared about ___ years later.

At the edge of Punjab, Alexander's advisers offer him three choices: (A) march on towards the Ganga with the army as it is; (B) camp where they stand and wait for fresh supplies while local tribes keep fighting; (C) turn back by the southern coastal route.
(a) What did Alexander's soldiers do about marching deeper, and what was their condition?
(b) What happened to his troops on the way back, and by which route?
(c) Which choice would you recommend? Use two facts from the chapter.
questions.a: (a) They refused to move deeper into India; they were tired, homesick and had lost the will to fight. (b) Heavy losses from thirst, hunger and disease on the coastal route in the south and through Iran's harsh desert. (c) Any reasoned choice citing two chapter facts: A risks facing fierce resistance with soldiers who refuse; B meets continuing resistance; C was what happened and brought heavy losses and rebellions back in Persia.
s: Part (a): refused to march on; tired and homesick
Part (b): heavy losses from thirst, hunger, disease on the coastal route
Part (c): a choice justified with two chapter facts

questions.q: A writer says Alexander's army was worn down on the way back from India by attacks from Indian rulers. Which fact in the chapter most directly weakens this?
questions.a: The retreat went by the coastal route in the south and Iran's harsh desert regions, and the chapter gives thirst, hunger and disease as the causes of the heavy losses. The wound, the women fighting and the soldiers' refusal belong to the campaign before the retreat and say nothing about its causes of loss.
o: Heavy losses on the retreat are put down to thirst, hunger and disease, not to battle
Alexander himself was seriously wounded in a battle against local tribes and rulers in India
In a few battles in India women fought side by side with their men against his army
His soldiers, tired and homesick, refused to move deeper into India towards the Ganga

questions.q:
News reaches Meher, a satrap at the far eastern edge of Alexander's empire, that Alexander has died in Babylon. Meher commands a strong army and rules a rich province, but he is very far from Babylon, and he knows nobody is there to stop him.
(a) Over how many continents did Alexander's empire spread at its height?
(b) What happened to the empire after Alexander's death?
(c) Why are far-off territories often the first to split away from an empire?
(d) Should Meher declare his province an independent kingdom or stay loyal to a general? Give a reasoned choice using the chapter.
questions.a: (a) Three continents. (b) It was divided between his generals and the satraps, who created their own kingdoms. (c) The larger an empire, the harder it is to hold together, and distant territories are hardest to control. (d) Either, with reasons: independence fits what the satraps did and the empire's fragility; staying loyal avoids war with generals nearer the centre.
s: Part (a): three continents
Part (b): divided between generals and satraps who made their own kingdoms
Part (c): large empires are hard to hold, far areas split first
Part (d): a justified decision using the chapter

questions.q: A school quiz says: 'Alexander's empire is among the largest in world history because he conquered the whole of India.' Which correction fits the chapter?
questions.a: The chapter says that after conquering the Persian Empire his empire spread over three continents, one of the largest in world history. In India he defeated Porus in Punjab but his soldiers refused to go further towards the Ganga and he retreated; Magadha and the Nandas were not his conquest.
o: Its size came from conquering Persia, across three continents; in India he beat Porus and turned back
Its size came from conquering Magadha and the Nanda empire, which he absorbed before returning to Persia
Its size came from the satraps, who conquered India for him after his death in Babylon at the age of 32
Its size came from conquering the whole of India and its coast, which his soldiers then refused to leave

questions.q: Rina says: 'Alexander matters in the history of India because he conquered the north and ruled it for a long time.' Is she right? Use the chapter in your answer.
questions.a: No. He defeated Porus in Punjab but met fierce resistance, his soldiers refused to go on, and he retreated, so his campaign had limited political impact in India. He is important in world history for conquering the Persian Empire and ruling one of the largest empires, and in India his campaign opened the door to Indo-Greek cultural contacts.
s: Verdict: not right, the political impact was limited
Evidence: resistance, refusing soldiers and retreat
What is true: world importance and Indo-Greek cultural contact

questions.q: Examine why Alexander's campaign in India ended without lasting conquest and what followed it.
questions.a: He defeated Porus in Punjab but met fierce resistance from local tribes and rulers, and was seriously wounded. His tired, homesick soldiers refused to go towards the Ganga, so he retreated, with heavy losses from thirst, hunger and disease. Back in Persia there were rebellions; he died in Babylon at 32, and his empire was divided among generals and satraps.
s: Fierce resistance from local tribes and rulers
Soldiers' refusal to march towards the Ganga
The retreat and heavy losses
Rebellions, death in Babylon at 32
Division of the empire; limited political impact

questions.q: A Greek coin is described in the chapter as 'probably showing Alexander on horseback attacking Porus on his elephant'. Which conclusion goes no further than the chapter allows?
questions.a: The chapter calls it a Greek coin that is 'probably' showing Alexander and Porus, so one may say only that it pictures a horseman attacking an elephant rider, with the identities not certain. The other options claim proofs of the result, of the Pauravas' tactics or of single combat, none of which the chapter says.
o: A Greek maker pictured a horseman attacking an elephant rider; the identities are only probable
The coin proves that Porus lost the battle while he was mounted on his elephant in the fight
The coin shows that the army of Porus fought only on elephants and never on horses or on foot
The coin proves that Alexander himself struck Porus down in single combat on the battlefield

questions.q: Alexander asked a sage, 'Which is stronger, life or death?' and was told, 'Life, because it endures while death does not.' He then asked, 'How can a man be most loved?' and was told, 'If he is most powerful and yet does not inspire fear.' (a) What makes the first reply an intelligent answer? (b) What hint was the second reply perhaps giving Alexander?
questions.a: (a) It gives a reason (life endures while death does not) instead of a bare choice. (b) It perhaps hinted to the mighty ruler that being loved needs power without making people afraid, which suited a king who had threatened sages with death.
s: Part (a): the answer comes with a reason
Part (b): power without inspiring fear, as a hint to the mighty ruler

questions.q:
Read the statements about Alexander.
Statement 1: After conquering the Persian Empire in 334-331 BCE, his empire spread over three continents.
Statement 2: His tired and homesick soldiers refused to move deeper into India towards the Ganga.
Statement 3: After he died in Babylon at the age of 32, his empire was soon divided between his generals and the satraps.
Which statements are correct?
questions.a: All three statements are correct: each is stated in the chapter (the conquest and three continents; the soldiers' refusal to go towards the Ganga; the death in Babylon at 32 and the division among generals and satraps).
o: 1, 2 and 3
1 and 3 only
1 and 2 only
2 and 3 only

questions.q: Which pair of facts from the chapter best explains why Alexander's Indian campaign had limited political impact?
questions.a: The chapter says he met fierce resistance and his tired, homesick soldiers refused to go deeper, so he retreated. Porus was defeated, not the victor; the Mauryas arose just after he left; and Greek cultural contact is the other effect, not a cause of the limit.
o: Fierce resistance from local tribes and rulers, and soldiers who would not go on
His defeat by Porus in Punjab, and the loss of his Persian lands to a rebellion there
His death in Babylon, and the capture of his army by the rulers of Magadha in the east
A treaty with the Maurya Empire, and the spread of Greek culture in the northern region

questions.q: Suppose Dhana Nanda had listened to Kautilya's warning and changed his ways. Which part of the chapter's account would then most directly fail to follow?
questions.a: The chapter says Kautilya advised Dhana Nanda to change his ways; angered, Dhana Nanda insulted him and threw him out, and this led to Kautilya's vow to end the Nanda rule. Had the advice been accepted, that link would be missing. Alexander's retreat and Megasthenes' stay do not depend on it, and the chapter gives no length for a Nanda dynasty that reformed.
o: Kautilya would not have been insulted and thrown out, so no vow to end Nanda rule would arise
Alexander would not have left India after his soldiers had refused to march any further east
Megasthenes would not have been hosted at a court in the great city of Pataliputra by the Ganga
The Nanda dynasty would have lasted as long as the Maurya Empire went on to last after them

questions.q:
The school library has a display about a book written by a Greek diplomat who stayed in an Indian court more than 2,000 years ago. A student wants to use the book to describe Maurya times in a project. Her teacher asks four questions.
(a) Name the book, its author and the king at whose court he stayed.
(b) Why can the full book not be read today?
(c) What do the king's friendly dealings with the author show about his relation with the Greeks?
(d) Should the student treat what is known of the book as a trustworthy source for her project? Give a reasoned judgement.
questions.a: (a) Indika, Megasthenes, Chandragupta Maurya. (b) It is lost except for excerpts quoted by later Greek scholars. (c) He defeated the Greek satraps but kept a diplomatic relationship with the Greeks. (d) Either, with reasons: it is the first written account by someone who lived there, so valuable; but it survives only through later quoting, so it should be checked against other sources.
s: Part (a): Indika, Megasthenes, Chandragupta
Part (b): lost except for quoted excerpts
Part (c): diplomatic relationship after defeating them
Part (d): a justified judgement on the source

questions.q: Which of these statements about the order of events in the chapter CANNOT be right?
questions.a: The chapter says Chandragupta hosted Megasthenes after he defeated the Greeks and kept a diplomatic relationship with them, so the first order is impossible. The other three orders match the chapter: the insult led to the vow, Magadha was taken before the satraps were defeated, and the Mauryas appeared around 321 BCE, a few years after Alexander left.
o: Megasthenes was hosted at the Maurya court before Chandragupta had defeated the Greek satraps
Kautilya was thrown out of Dhana Nanda's court before he took his vow to end the Nanda rule
Chandragupta took control of Magadha before he defeated the Greek satraps left by Alexander
The Maurya Empire emerged a few years after Alexander had left India with his army

questions.q: (a) The chapter says there are many stories about Chandragupta's origin and adventures. What do they have in common? (b) Why can a historian rely more on this common point than on any one story?
questions.a: (a) They agree that he overthrew the Nandas and took control of Magadha, establishing his rule with Pataliputra as capital. (b) A detail on which many different stories agree is less likely to be a single storyteller's invention than a detail found in only one version.
s: Part (a): overthrew the Nandas and took Magadha with Pataliputra as capital
Part (b): agreement among many stories makes a point more reliable

questions.q:
A school history club builds a timeline: Ashoka is Chandragupta's grandson, and the chapter dates his reign from 268 BCE. The Maurya Empire began around 321 BCE. The club also notes that Chandragupta had a Greek visitor in his court and an adviser who had once taught at Takshashila.
(a) Name the adviser and the Greek visitor.
(b) How many years separate 321 BCE from the start of Ashoka's reign, and does that fit the relationship of grandfather and grandson?
(c) Which group left behind by Alexander did Chandragupta defeat?
(d) The club must label the Maurya gallery either 'Built by a Brilliant Mentor' or 'Built on Magadha's Resources'. Which would you choose, and why?
questions.a: (a) Kautilya (Chanakya or Vishnugupta) and Megasthenes. (b) 321 - 268 = 53 years, which fits two generations. (c) The Greek satraps in the north-west. (d) Either, with reasons: Kautilya's advice and strategy; or Magadha's geography, economic system and trade.
s: Part (a): Kautilya and Megasthenes
Part (b): 53 years and a sensible comment on two generations
Part (c): Greek satraps
Part (d): a justified label using the chapter

questions.q:
Read the statements about the founding of the Maurya Empire.
Statement 1: The Maurya Empire emerged around 321 BCE, a few years after Alexander left India.
Statement 2: Chandragupta's empire stretched from the northern plains to the Deccan plateau, but the north-west stayed under the Greek satraps.
Statement 3: Chandragupta kept a diplomatic relationship with the Greeks and hosted Megasthenes in his court.
Which statements are correct?
questions.a: Statements 1 and 3 are correct. Statement 2 is false: the chapter says Chandragupta defeated the Greek satraps left behind in the north-west and integrated the region into his empire.
o: 1 and 3 only
1 and 2 only
2 and 3 only
1, 2 and 3

questions.q: Mohan says: 'Chandragupta's expansion owed as much to Magadha's advantages as to Kautilya's advice.' Do you agree? Give reasons.
questions.a: Yes, broadly. The chapter says Magadha's geography, an established economic system and flourishing trade, combined with the advice of the master strategist Kautilya, helped Chandragupta gradually expand his empire. It does not say which mattered more, so 'as much' is a fair reading.
s: Verdict: agrees, with care
Reason: Magadha's geography, economic system and trade
Reason: Kautilya's strategic advice; the chapter links both

questions.q: The chapter says 'according to Buddhist texts' Kautilya was a teacher at Takshashila, and 'as per many accounts' Chandragupta succeeded with Kautilya's help. (a) Why does the chapter use these phrases instead of stating them flatly? (b) Name one kind of source that a historian would look for to check them.
questions.a: (a) The chapter names its sources ('according to Buddhist texts', 'as per many accounts'), which signals that these claims rest on particular accounts and not on direct proof. (b) Any sensible check such as another account or text, an inscription, a coin or an eyewitness record like Megasthenes' book.
s: Part (a): the information rests on accounts and texts, so the source is named
Part (b): another kind of source suggested for checking

questions.q: 'Chandragupta's success was the result of favourable conditions and wise counsel together.' Justify this statement using the chapter.
questions.a: Magadha's geography, established economy and flourishing trade gave a strong base. The Nanda ruler was unpopular, making his empire weak. Kautilya, the master strategist, advised Chandragupta. With these, Chandragupta overthrew the Nandas, made Pataliputra his capital, defeated the Greek satraps and built an empire from the northern plains to the Deccan.
s: Magadha's geography and economy as a base
Dhana Nanda's unpopularity
Kautilya's advice as strategist
Overthrow of the Nandas and Pataliputra as capital
Defeat of the satraps and the extent of the empire

questions.q: The chapter tells how Dhana Nanda insulted Kautilya and Kautilya vowed to end Nanda rule, and how Kautilya later guided Chandragupta. Analyse the two decisions that changed Magadha's history, Dhana Nanda's decision to throw out the adviser and Kautilya's decision to back Chandragupta, and judge which was the more important turning point.
questions.a: Dhana Nanda, though very rich and unpopular, angered by the warning, insulted Kautilya and threw him out, which led to Kautilya's vow to end Nanda rule. Kautilya, who used his knowledge of politics, governance and economics, then helped Chandragupta overthrow the Nandas and expand. A reasoned judgement is accepted: Dhana Nanda's decision created the enemy, but without Kautilya's strategy joined to Magadha's geography, economy and trade, the vow alone would not have built an empire; or the reverse, that without the insult Kautilya would have had no reason to act.
s: Dhana Nanda's decision and its effect (insult, vow)
Kautilya's decision and what he used (strategy, knowledge) to help Chandragupta
A turning point is chosen clearly
First reason from the chapter for the choice
Second reason, or why the other decision mattered less

questions.q:
Match each item in Column I with the part it played for Chandragupta in Column II.
Column I: 1. Dhana Nanda's unpopularity  2. Kautilya's knowledge of politics, governance and economics  3. Magadha's established economic system and trade  4. The region of the Greek satraps
Column II: a. A base of resources and income for his expansion  b. A weakness in the empire he overthrew  c. A strategist's skill used to create his empire  d. Territory he defeated and integrated into his empire
questions.a: Dhana Nanda's unpopularity paved the way for the Nanda empire to be conquered; Kautilya used his knowledge of politics, governance and economics to create the empire; Magadha's geography, economic system and trade gave a base; and the Greek satraps' region in the north-west was defeated and integrated.

questions.q: Suppose Chandragupta had Kautilya's advice but ruled a small hill kingdom with no trade. (a) Which advantages of Magadha would he lack? (b) What does the chapter suggest about how far advice alone could have taken him?
questions.a: (a) Magadha's geography, its established economic system and its flourishing trade. (b) The chapter says these advantages combined with Kautilya's advice helped him expand, so advice alone would probably not have been enough.
s: Part (a): geography, economic system, flourishing trade
Part (b): the chapter ties his expansion to advice together with those advantages

questions.q: A pupil labels a sketch of the Maurya Empire under Chandragupta as covering 'only Magadha'. Which fact in the chapter best shows the label is too small?
questions.a: Only the defeat and integration of the satraps' region, with an empire stretching from the northern plains to the Deccan plateau, speaks of extent. The visit of Megasthenes, Kautilya's teaching post and Magadha's advantages are true but do not tell how far the empire reached.
o: He defeated the Greek satraps and integrated the north-west into an empire reaching the Deccan plateau
He hosted the Greek diplomat Megasthenes at his court in the capital city of Pataliputra on the Ganga
His mentor Kautilya had been a teacher at the world-renowned university of Takshashila in the north-west
Magadha already had good geography, an established economy and a flourishing trade in its Ganga plains

questions.q: A project list of people connected with Chandragupta's court reads: Kautilya, Chanakya, Vishnugupta and Megasthenes. Going by the chapter, the number of different people on this list is ___.
A pupil says: 'The chapter shows that Alexander's invasion caused the Maurya Empire to be founded, since it began only a few years after he left.' Which comment fits the chapter?
questions.a: The chapter dates the Maurya Empire to around 321 BCE, just a few years after Alexander left India, and explains Chandragupta's expansion by Magadha's geography, economic system and trade together with Kautilya's advice. It never makes the invasion the cause; the satraps were enemies Chandragupta later defeated.
o: It gives the timing but credits Magadha's advantages and Kautilya's advice; it never says the invasion caused it
She is right, because the chapter says the invasion weakened the Nandas and so opened the way for the Mauryas
She is right, because the chapter says Alexander left Chandragupta in charge of the satraps in the north-west
She is wrong, because the chapter says the Maurya Empire emerged long before Alexander ever came to India

questions.q: Imagine Megasthenes writes a three-line diary entry on reaching the Indian court. Write it so that it shows who hosts him, where the court is, and what he plans to write.
questions.a: An entry such as: 'I reached Pataliputra, capital of Chandragupta Maurya. The king, who defeated our satraps, still keeps friendly ties with us and welcomes me. I will write all I see in a book on India.' It names the host, the capital and the plan for Indika.
s: Names Chandragupta as host
Names Pataliputra as the capital
States plan to write an account (Indika)

questions.q: A museum wants a label on Chandragupta that stays within the chapter, which says there are many stories of his origin and adventures. Which label does so?
questions.a: The chapter says the common theme of the many stories is that he overthrew the Nandas and took control of Magadha, establishing his rule with Pataliputra as capital. The other labels state origins, teachers or victories the chapter does not give.
o: Chandragupta Maurya overthrew the Nandas, took Magadha and ruled from Pataliputra; stories of his origins differ
Chandragupta Maurya was a Nanda prince who inherited the throne of Magadha directly from Dhana Nanda
Chandragupta Maurya studied at Takshashila under Dhana Nanda, then went on to take over Magadha
Chandragupta Maurya defeated Alexander in Punjab and then went on to found the city of Pataliputra

questions.q: A courtier says Chandragupta should have moved his capital to the north-west after defeating the Greek satraps there. (a) Using the chapter's description of a capital and its account of Magadha, give one reason for keeping Pataliputra. (b) Which act of Chandragupta in the chapter shows that he still did not neglect the north-west?
questions.a: (a) A capital is usually a major centre of economic and administrative power, and Pataliputra lay in Magadha, with its geography, established economic system and flourishing trade. (b) He defeated the Greek satraps left behind there and integrated the region into his empire.
s: Part (a): capital as centre of economic and administrative power, with Magadha's advantages
Part (b): defeated the satraps and integrated the north-west

questions.q: Describe, in the order the chapter gives them, three steps by which Chandragupta moved from overthrowing the Nandas to ruling an empire from the northern plains to the Deccan, and say what each step added to his power.
questions.a: First he overthrew the Nandas and took control of Magadha with Pataliputra as capital, which gave him Magadha's geography, established economy and trade. Then he defeated the Greek satraps left by Alexander in the north-west and integrated the region, which extended his empire. Afterwards he maintained a diplomatic relationship with the Greeks and hosted Megasthenes, which kept peaceful dealings with them.
s: Overthrow of the Nandas and Magadha with its advantages
Defeat of the satraps and integration of the north-west
Diplomatic relationship with the Greeks and Megasthenes

questions.q: (a) Is it a contradiction that a king who defeated Alexander's satraps then hosted a Greek diplomat in his court? Give a reason from the chapter. (b) What did the defeat add to his empire?
questions.a: (a) No: he defeated the Greek satraps left behind in the north-west, but afterwards kept a diplomatic relationship with the Greeks, so the two actions were about different things. (b) The north-west region was integrated into an empire stretching from the northern plains to the Deccan plateau.
s: Part (a): defeated satraps yet kept a diplomatic relationship, so no contradiction
Part (b): integration of the north-west into the empire

questions.q:
Assertion (A): Our knowledge of Megasthenes' account comes only from passages quoted by later Greek scholars.
Reason (R): Megasthenes wrote Indika after leaving India, without ever having been to Chandragupta's court.
Choose the correct option.
questions.a: The Assertion is true: Indika is lost except for excerpts quoted by later Greek scholars. The Reason is false: the chapter says Chandragupta hosted Megasthenes in his court and that he wrote about his travels in India.
o: The Assertion is true, but the Reason is false.
Both Assertion and Reason are true, and the Reason is the correct explanation of the Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true, but the Reason is not the correct explanation of the Assertion.
The Assertion is false, but the Reason is true.

questions.q: True or False: In the saptanga, 'janapada' means only the people of the state, and the land they live on is counted under the treasury. Give the correct statement if false.
questions.a: False. Janapada is the territory of the state along with the population inhabiting it; the treasury (kosha) is the wealth of the kingdom, a separate part.
s: Verdict: False
